summary: John White's proposal for a Network Mail Protocol, a far richer replacement for the two FTP mail commands MAIL and MLFL. It is explicitly a request for comments rather than a final specification, and invites bug reports and position papers.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 524 proposes a Mail Protocol (MP) inside FTP that goes beyond sending a file or text to one local user. It describes functions for delivery, distribution, forwarding, permanent records, citation updates, and identity checks, while asking readers to report problems.

questions: what are the mp mail functions
subtitle: A proposed mail subsystem for FTP with delivery, forwarding, recording, and verification functions.

tldr.problem: The existing FTP MAIL and MLFL commands could send text or a file to a local recipient, but the author wanted a richer system for delivering, recording, forwarding, and managing network mail.
tldr.mechanism: The proposed Mail Protocol (MP) is a command subsystem entered from FTP with MAIL. It defines seven functions and lets a server implement any, all, or none of them.
tldr.outcome: RFC 524 explicitly asks for comments and reports that the proposal may contain bugs; it is not presented as a final specification.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 524's status as Unknown and no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC itself calls MP a proposed protocol and explicitly requests comments and bug reports.

sections.title: A Mail Subsystem Inside FTP
sections.content:
John White presents MP as a proposed network mail protocol. At the time described, FTP's MAIL and MLFL commands let an FTP user process send a file or text string to an FTP server for a local recipient. MP is intended to support a broader set of mail functions.

Mail is defined as text communicated between human users or processes in less than real time. MP is accessed from the FTP command space with MAIL and left with EXIT. While inside MP, the server accepts MP commands and rejects FTP commands. The RFC calls itself a request for comments and asks readers to report bugs and concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: MP is a proposed set of mail commands available inside FTP. A user enters it with MAIL, performs a mail task, and returns to FTP with EXIT.

sections.title: Mail, Agents, and Recorded Messages
sections.content:
The proposal distinguishes unrecorded mail, which is delivered without permanent storage, from recorded mail, whose citation is kept by a Recording Agent and can be retrieved later by pathname. A Recording Agent stores the message's citation and assigns its pathname. A Distribution Agent accepts mail for recipients at other hosts, tries to deliver it, and can send acknowledgments to a Monitor.

A recorded message has static attributes, such as content, title, authors, clerk, and creation date, that stay fixed after recording. Its dynamic attributes include distribution, access, and catalog lists, which a person with Controlling Access may modify. Read Access allows retrieval of content; Controlling Access allows changes to dynamic attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Some mail is sent and then discarded, while recorded mail receives a pathname and can be kept for later retrieval. The proposal also separates permission to read a record from permission to change its lists.

sections.title: The Seven Mail Functions
sections.content:
MP defines seven functions: Recording, Delivery, Distribution, Forwarding, Citation Retrieval, Update Citation, and User Verification. Recording stores a message; Delivery sends it to recipients; Distribution asks an intermediary to deliver it, potentially across hosts; and Forwarding passes delivered but unread mail to another individual.

Citation Retrieval returns selected information about recorded mail, and Update Citation changes dynamic attributes when the requestor has permission. User Verification checks whether an ID belongs to a named individual. A host may implement any, all, or none of these functions. The RFC assigns reply 400 when a function is not implemented and 332 when login is required.
sections.plainLanguage: The functions cover sending, distributing, and forwarding mail; storing and retrieving records; changing record access; and checking a user's identity. A server can support only the functions it implements.

sections.title: Delivery Reports and the Worked Example
sections.content:
For Distribution, a sender can specify recipients, acknowledgment conditions, a cutoff interval, report interval, and a Monitor. The default acknowledgment condition is FAILURE, so an acknowledgment is sent if at least one delivery fails. The default cutoff is 7 days; after that, attempts to recipients not yet reached are abandoned. Delivery status can be SUCCESSFUL, FAILED, WAITING, TIMED OUT, or UNATTEMPTED.

The worked example records a public message at the NIC, receives pathname 15490, and then distributes it to one recipient. It requests an acknowledgment whether delivery succeeds or fails, asks for a terse acknowledgment, and sets a one-day cutoff. The RFC presents this as an example of NIC Journal Submission.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender can ask a Distribution Agent to try delivery, report failures, and stop after a chosen interval. The example stores a message first, then asks the agent to deliver it and report the result.
